parts.label: Temperature
parts.note: This axis tracks the temperature of the substance, so we can watch when it climbs and when it stays stubbornly flat.

parts.label: Energy added
parts.note: Moving right, we keep pumping in energy; the graph shows what that energy does to the substance as it arrives.

parts.label: Solid warming up
parts.note: Here the solid soaks up energy and its particles vibrate faster, so the line climbs steadily as temperature rises.

parts.label: Melting (latent heat of fusion)
parts.note: The line goes flat: energy now melts the solid into liquid, no temperature rise, using the latent heat of fusion.

parts.label: Boiling (latent heat of vaporisation)
parts.note: A second, longer flat section: energy boils liquid into gas, using the much larger latent heat of vaporisation.

parts.label: Bonds breaking, temp constant
parts.note: During each flat bit, incoming energy pulls particles apart rather than speeding them up, so the temperature holds steady.

parts.label: Heated block
parts.note: We start with a block of known mass — pumping energy in raises its temperature, and how much it needs tells us its specific heat capacity.

parts.label: Insulation
parts.note: We wrap the block in insulation so heat stays inside instead of leaking to the surroundings, making the measured temperature rise more accurate.

parts.label: Electric heater
parts.note: The electric heater slots into the block and delivers a steady flow of energy, warming it from the inside out.

parts.label: Thermometer
parts.note: A thermometer sits in the block to track its temperature rise, so we know exactly how many degrees the energy warmed it by.

parts.label: Power supply
parts.note: The power supply drives current through the heater; its power multiplied by the heating time gives the total energy supplied.

parts.label: Joulemeter
parts.note: The joulemeter counts the energy flowing into the heater, so we can divide it by mass and temperature rise to find c.

parts.label: pH scale
parts.note: We lay out a number line from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, so we can compare them.

parts.label: Universal indicator
parts.note: Adding universal indicator turns the solution a colour, and matching that colour to the chart tells us the pH straight away.

parts.label: Acidic (H+)
parts.note: Down the low end sit acids: they release hydrogen ions (H+) into the water, and more H+ means a lower pH, redder colour.

parts.label: Neutral pH 7
parts.note: Right in the middle at pH 7 the H+ and OH- have cancelled, combining as H+ + OH- making water, leaving a neutral salt solution.

parts.label: Alkaline (OH-)
parts.note: Up the high end sit alkalis: they release hydroxide ions (OH-), pushing the pH above 7 towards the purple end.

parts.label: Reactants
parts.note: We start with the reactants sitting here, holding chemical energy in their bonds, ready to react and rearrange into new substances.

parts.label: Activation energy
parts.note: First we climb this energy hill: activation energy is put in to break the starting bonds before any new bonds can form.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: New products settle here, lower down, because making their bonds released more energy than breaking the old bonds took in.

parts.label: Energy released
parts.note: The drop from reactants to products is energy dumped into the surroundings, warming them up, like in combustion or a hand warmer.

parts.label: Endothermic profile
parts.note: Now the endothermic case: products end up higher than reactants, so this reaction has soaked up energy overall.

parts.label: Energy taken in
parts.note: This upward gap is energy pulled in from the surroundings, cooling them down, as a sports cold pack chills an injury.

parts.label: Chromatography paper (stationary phase)
parts.note: The paper stays still as the stationary phase, holding onto each dye more or less strongly as the solvent creeps up it.

parts.label: Solvent (mobile phase)
parts.note: The solvent soaks up the paper as the mobile phase, carrying the dissolved substances along with it as it rises.

parts.label: Pencil baseline
parts.note: We mark the start line in pencil, not ink, so it won't dissolve and run up the paper, spoiling our measurement.

parts.label: Solvent front
parts.note: The highest point the solvent reaches; we mark it fast before it dries, as it's the bottom of our Rf sum.

parts.label: Separated spot
parts.note: Each substance travels its own distance and separates into a spot, because some cling to the paper while others race up with the solvent.

parts.label: Distance moved (Rf)
parts.note: We divide the spot's distance by the solvent's distance to get the Rf value, always between 0 and 1, to identify the substance.

parts.label: Hydrogen: squeaky pop
parts.note: Hold a lighted splint at the tube mouth: the hydrogen ignites suddenly, giving that tell-tale squeaky pop as it burns.

parts.label: Oxygen: relights splint
parts.note: Push a glowing splint into the gas: oxygen feeds the embers so fiercely the flame bursts back to life and relights.

parts.label: Limewater turns milky
parts.note: Bubble the gas through clear limewater: carbon dioxide reacts with it, forming a solid that turns the liquid cloudy and milky.

parts.label: Chlorine: bleaches litmus
parts.note: Hold damp litmus paper in the gas: chlorine strips out its colour, bleaching the paper white to reveal itself.

parts.label: Splint
parts.note: A thin wooden splint is your basic tool here — lit or glowing, it reacts differently depending on which gas surrounds it.

parts.label: Crude oil in
parts.note: Crude oil, a finite mixture of hydrocarbon chains of many different lengths, is pumped in ready to be separated.

parts.label: Fractionating column
parts.note: The mixture is heated so it evaporates, then the vapours rise up this tall tower to be split into useful fractions.

parts.label: Cool top
parts.note: Up here it's coolest, so only the lightest vapours reach this far before condensing back into liquid and being tapped off.

parts.label: Short-chain fraction
parts.note: Short chains have low boiling points, so they rise highest as vapour; runny, volatile and flammable, ideal for fuels like petrol.

parts.label: Long-chain fraction
parts.note: Long chains have high boiling points, so they barely rise and drain out low down; thick, sticky liquids like bitumen.

parts.label: Hot bottom (furnace)
parts.note: The furnace heats the base hardest, boiling the mixture so vapours rise and each fraction condenses where the tower cools enough.

parts.label: Large hydrocarbon
parts.note: A long, less useful hydrocarbon chain arrives from crude oil, ready to be broken down into smaller molecules people actually want.

parts.label: Hot catalyst
parts.note: The big molecule is heated and passed over a hot catalyst, which snaps the long chain apart into shorter pieces.

parts.label: Small alkane (fuel)
parts.note: Out comes a short-chain alkane, a saturated molecule burned as fuel like petrol, meeting the high demand for fuels.

parts.label: Alkene
parts.note: The leftover piece is an alkene, a shorter unsaturated molecule that becomes a building block for making polymers like plastics.

parts.label: C=C double bond
parts.note: Two carbons share a double bond here, so the molecule holds fewer hydrogens (CnH2n) and is far more reactive than an alkane.

parts.label: Bromine water test
parts.note: Shake the alkene with orange bromine water and its double bond grabs the bromine, turning the mixture colourless to prove it is unsaturated.

parts.label: Balance beam
parts.note: The beam sits level to show the reaction's total mass never changes: atoms are only rearranged, never made or destroyed.

parts.label: Reactants
parts.note: We load the starting chemicals onto this side; these atoms will be shuffled into new arrangements during the reaction.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: The new substances land here, built from exactly the same atoms, so this pan weighs the same as the reactants.

parts.label: Atoms (same on both sides)
parts.note: Count each type of atom: the numbers match on both sides, which is why the beam stays perfectly balanced.

parts.label: Gas escaping (mass falls)
parts.note: A gas bubbles off into the air and drifts away, so the mass left on the pan seems to drop.

parts.label: Gas taken in (mass rises)
parts.note: Gas from the air joins the solid, like a metal rusting, so extra atoms are added and the mass seems to climb.

parts.label: Balance (mass)
parts.note: The balance weighs out an exact mass of substance; divide that mass by the relative formula mass to count how many moles you have.

parts.label: Solute
parts.note: This is the solid you dissolve; weighing it lets you work out what fraction of its mass is each element inside the compound.

parts.label: Solution
parts.note: As the solute dissolves it spreads through the liquid, making a solution whose concentration is that dissolved mass divided by the volume.

parts.label: Solvent (water)
parts.note: Water is added as the solvent to dissolve the solute; more water for the same mass gives a lower concentration in g/dm cubed.

parts.label: Meniscus
parts.note: The liquid curves at the surface; read the bottom of this meniscus at eye level so your volume measurement is accurate and repeatable.

parts.label: Volume scale
parts.note: These marks let you read the volume, but every reading carries some uncertainty, so measure carefully and repeat to improve reliability.

parts.label: Reactant particles
parts.note: We start with reactant particles zipping about, each carrying energy and needing to meet another to react.

parts.label: Collision
parts.note: Two particles smash together with enough energy and the right angle, so old bonds break and the reaction happens.

parts.label: Product particles
parts.note: That successful collision rearranges the atoms, and out come the product particles the reaction was making.

parts.label: Faster particles (heat)
parts.note: Heating gives particles more energy, so they zoom faster and collide more often and harder, speeding the reaction up.

parts.label: Activation energy
parts.note: Collisions only work if they clear this energy barrier; below it particles just bounce off without reacting.

parts.label: Catalyst pathway
parts.note: A catalyst opens a lower-energy route over the barrier, so more collisions succeed, yet it emerges unchanged itself.

parts.label: Closed system
parts.note: Seal everything in a closed container so nothing escapes; this lets the forward and reverse reactions balance and settle into equilibrium.

parts.label: Reactants
parts.note: The starting substances go in on the left; once at equilibrium their amount stays steady even though they keep reacting.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: The new substances build up on the right, but they don't run out or pile up endlessly because their amount now holds constant.

parts.label: Forward reaction
parts.note: Reactants turn into products, racing left to right; this forward change happens at exactly the same rate as the reverse one.

parts.label: Reverse reaction
parts.note: Meanwhile products change back into reactants, running right to left, so nothing truly stops; the two directions just cancel out.

parts.label: Reversible arrow
parts.note: The special double arrow replaces the single one, signalling the reaction runs both ways so products can reform the original reactants.

parts.label: Atmosphere (N₂ + O₂)
parts.note: The air we breathe today settles at roughly 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen, plus traces of carbon dioxide and noble gases.

parts.label: Volcano (CO₂ + steam)
parts.note: Erupting volcanoes belch out carbon dioxide and steam, filling the early atmosphere with gases but almost no oxygen.

parts.label: Ocean
parts.note: As Earth cools, that volcanic steam condenses into rain, collecting on the surface to form the first oceans.

parts.label: Algae
parts.note: Algae in the oceans photosynthesise, releasing oxygen that slowly builds up and begins changing the atmosphere.

parts.label: Plants
parts.note: Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, pulling it from the air and releasing yet more oxygen.

parts.label: Sedimentary rock
parts.note: Dead organisms and dissolved carbon dioxide get buried, locking carbon into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels underground.

parts.label: Sun
parts.note: The Sun pours energy at the Earth as light, the free heat source that drives our whole climate system.

parts.label: Incoming sunlight
parts.note: Sunlight streams down through the atmosphere and warms the ground, land and sea soaking up its energy.

parts.label: Greenhouse gases
parts.note: Gases like carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour form a blanket that traps outgoing heat, keeping Earth warm enough for life.

parts.label: Re-emitted infrared
parts.note: The warm Earth radiates heat back as infrared; greenhouse gases absorb it instead of letting it escape to space.

parts.label: Burning fossil fuels
parts.note: Burning fossil fuels pumps extra carbon dioxide into the air, thickening the blanket and driving global warming.

parts.label: Soot (particulates)
parts.note: Incomplete burning also throws out soot particulates that dirty the air and can trigger breathing problems.

parts.label: Acid rain
parts.note: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain clouds, falling as acid rain that damages buildings, trees and lakes.

parts.label: Fresh water source
parts.note: We start with fresh water from a river or reservoir; it looks clean but carries mud, grit and microbes we must remove.

parts.label: Filtration
parts.note: The water trickles through beds of sand and gravel that trap solid bits, so insoluble dirt is left behind and the water clears.

parts.label: Sterilising
parts.note: Next we kill remaining microbes by adding chlorine or bubbling ozone, or shining ultraviolet light through, making the water safe to drink.

parts.label: Potable water
parts.note: Out comes potable water, safe to drink; it still holds dissolved salts, so it is safe but not chemically pure.

parts.label: Desalination
parts.note: Where fresh water is scarce, we feed in salty seawater instead and desalinate it, though this step swallows a lot of energy.

parts.label: Sedimentation tank
parts.note: In waste-water treatment, sewage sits still in a tank so heavy solids sink out as sludge, separating it from the liquid above.

parts.label: Reverse osmosis
parts.note: Here the salty water is forced under high pressure through a membrane that blocks the salt, letting only pure water squeeze through.

parts.label: Raw materials
parts.note: The story starts here: we dig up or grow the raw materials, tracking the energy used and habitats disturbed to extract them.

parts.label: Manufacture
parts.note: Next, factories turn those raw materials into the product, burning energy and often releasing pollutants we must add to the tally.

parts.label: Use product
parts.note: Now the product is used, sometimes for years; any energy, water or waste it needs while working also counts in the assessment.

parts.label: Disposal
parts.note: At the end, the product is thrown away, burned or buried, so we weigh up the waste and pollution its disposal creates.

parts.label: Recycle loop
parts.note: Instead of dumping it, we can loop the material back to be reused or recycled, saving resources and energy since recycling metal beats extracting fresh ore.

parts.label: Bias / judgement
parts.note: Some impacts, like pollution effects, are hard to measure and judged differently, so an LCA can be tilted to make a product look greener than it is.

parts.label: Measuring cylinder
parts.note: We start with a measuring cylinder: its scale lets us read off a volume of liquid precisely, in cubic centimetres.

parts.label: Water
parts.note: Pour in water and note the starting level. This water will do the measuring for us when the solid goes in.

parts.label: Irregular solid
parts.note: Lower in an odd-shaped solid you can't measure with a ruler. It sinks and pushes the water aside to make room.

parts.label: Displaced level
parts.note: The water rises: the volume it climbs by exactly equals the solid's volume, since it shoved that much water out of the way.

parts.label: Balance
parts.note: Now we weigh the solid on a balance to find its mass in grams, the top number in the density sum.

parts.label: Regular solid
parts.note: For a neat block, skip the water: measure its sides with a ruler and multiply to get volume, then divide mass by it.

parts.label: Floating object
parts.note: Drop an object in liquid and it floats if it's less dense: gram-for-gram it's lighter than the water it would replace.

parts.label: Solid
parts.note: We start cold: particles locked in a fixed regular pattern, only vibrating on the spot, so the solid holds its shape.

parts.label: Liquid
parts.note: Add energy and bonds loosen: particles now slip and slide past each other, so the liquid flows and takes its container's shape.

parts.label: Gas
parts.note: Add more energy still: particles break free and zoom apart in all directions, spreading out to fill whatever space they're in.

parts.label: Melting / Freezing
parts.note: Heating in melts solid to liquid; cooling reverses it, freezing liquid back to solid and giving that energy out again.

parts.label: Boiling / Condensing
parts.note: Boiling takes energy in to fling liquid particles into gas; condensing gives it out as gas collapses back to liquid.

parts.label: Sublimation
parts.note: Sometimes a solid skips liquid entirely, taking energy in to jump straight to gas — like dry ice smoking away.

parts.label: Container
parts.note: The gas is trapped inside sealed walls. Every particle is bouncing about, and it is those walls the particles will keep hitting.

parts.label: Gas particle
parts.note: One tiny particle zooms across the space, moving in a straight line until it strikes something. Billions of these are racing around at once.

parts.label: Collision with wall
parts.note: The particle slams into the wall and bounces back. Each tiny push adds up over billions of hits, and that total force is the pressure.

parts.label: Piston (movable wall)
parts.note: This wall slides in, squashing the gas smaller. The particles now hit it more often, so the pressure pushing back climbs higher.

parts.label: Pushing in / doing work
parts.note: Pushing the piston does work on the gas, handing energy to the particles. They speed up and warm the gas, even with no heating.

parts.label: System
parts.note: We draw a boundary to pick out the objects we're studying; energy moves between stores inside, or across this line to the surroundings.

parts.label: Energy store
parts.note: Inside the system, energy starts filled up in one store here, ready to be shifted somewhere else in the process.

parts.label: Second store
parts.note: The energy has to arrive somewhere, so a second store fills up as the first one empties out.

parts.label: Transfer
parts.note: Energy flows from the first store to the second, carried across mechanically, electrically, by heating, or by radiation like light and sound.

parts.label: Wasted energy
parts.note: As the transfer happens, some energy leaks away as wasted heat, spreading out and no longer useful to us.

parts.label: Surroundings
parts.note: The wasted energy warms the surroundings, but nothing is lost overall; the total energy across everything stays exactly the same.

parts.label: GPE store
parts.note: The raised object holds a full gravitational store: lift it higher or make it heavier and this store grows, ready to be spent.

parts.label: Height (h)
parts.note: The height above the ground sets how much is stored, since energy equals mass times gravitational field strength times this height.

parts.label: Object falls
parts.note: As it drops, the gravitational store empties and pours into the kinetic store, with the total energy staying the same throughout.

parts.label: Kinetic store
parts.note: The object speeds up as it falls, filling its kinetic store; double the speed and the store grows four times, since speed is squared.

parts.label: Work done
parts.note: Gravity does work by pulling the object through a distance, and this work is exactly how the energy gets transferred, measured in joules.

parts.label: Spring extension
parts.note: Stretching the spring stores energy elastically; pull it further and the extension grows, so long as it springs back to its original length.

parts.label: Elastic PE
parts.note: The stretched spring now holds an elastic store; released, it snaps back and pushes this energy into the object's kinetic store.

parts.label: Input energy
parts.note: Energy flows into the device every second; how fast it arrives is the power, measured in joules per second (watts).

parts.label: Device
parts.note: Inside the device, the input energy is transferred into different forms; how well it does this is its efficiency.

parts.label: Useful output
parts.note: Some energy leaves as the useful transfer we actually want; the bigger this share, the more efficient the device.

parts.label: Wasted (dissipated) energy
parts.note: The rest is dissipated to the surroundings, usually as heat; this is why no device can ever reach 100% efficient.

parts.label: Insulation
parts.note: Insulation with low thermal conductivity wraps the device, slowing heat escaping so less useful energy is wasted.

parts.label: Lubricated part
parts.note: Oil between moving parts cuts friction, so less energy is wasted as heat and more becomes useful output.

parts.label: Thick wall
parts.note: A thicker wall of low-conductivity material slows heat passing through, trapping warmth and reducing wasted energy transfer.

parts.label: Wind turbine
parts.note: Moving air pushes the blades round, spinning a generator to make electricity — and the wind keeps blowing, so it never runs out.

parts.label: Solar panel
parts.note: Sunlight falls on the panel and is turned straight into electricity — a renewable supply that's topped up every day the sun shines.

parts.label: Hydroelectric dam
parts.note: Water held behind the dam rushes down through turbines, spinning them to generate electricity from the never-ending rain cycle.

parts.label: Pylon (electricity grid)
parts.note: Pylons carry the electricity along the grid, delivering it from every power source to homes, schools and factories that need it.

parts.label: Fossil-fuel power station
parts.note: Here coal, oil or gas is burned to boil water; the steam spins turbines — reliable, high-energy, but the fuel eventually runs out.

parts.label: CO2 emissions
parts.note: Burning fossil fuels sends carbon dioxide into the air, a greenhouse gas warming the planet — the very reason we're shifting to renewables.

parts.label: Object
parts.note: Here is the object sitting still on a surface; several forces push and pull on it at once, and we track each one.

parts.label: Normal contact force
parts.note: The surface pushes straight up on the object, a contact force balancing it so it does not sink downward through the ground.

parts.label: Weight (W = mg)
parts.note: Gravity pulls the whole mass downward; multiply the mass by gravitational field strength (W = mg) to get this downward weight force.

parts.label: Centre of mass
parts.note: Weight acts from this single balance point, the centre of mass, so we draw the whole arrow starting neatly from here.

parts.label: Resultant force
parts.note: Add the forces together: here the up and down forces cancel, so the resultant is zero and the object stays still.

parts.label: Resolved component
parts.note: A slanted force is split into two perpendicular parts, letting us handle each direction separately and find the true resultant.

parts.label: Spring
parts.note: This coiled spring hangs from a stand, ready to stretch when we load it — the object whose stiffness we are measuring.

parts.label: Mass (force)
parts.note: We hang known masses on the spring; their weight pulls down, providing the measured force that stretches the spring further.

parts.label: Ruler
parts.note: A ruler beside the spring lets us read how far the bottom moves, measuring the stretch caused by each added weight.

parts.label: Extension
parts.note: Extension is how much longer the spring gets; doubling the force doubles it, so together they give the spring constant k.

parts.label: Hooke's law (linear)
parts.note: Here force and extension climb in a straight line: F equals k times e, so the spring stretches steadily and springs back.

parts.label: Limit of proportionality
parts.note: Past this point the line bends: the spring is overstretched and deforms inelastically, no longer springing fully back when unloaded.

parts.label: Distance axis
parts.note: We plot distance up the side; as the object travels, its position climbs higher and higher up this axis over time.

parts.label: Time axis
parts.note: Time runs along the bottom, always moving forward; every point across shows how far the object has got by that moment.

parts.label: Gradient = speed
parts.note: The steepness of the line tells you the speed: a steeper slope means more distance covered each second, so the object is moving faster.

parts.label: Flat (stationary)
parts.note: When the line goes flat, distance stops rising even though time ticks on, so the object is stationary, just waiting.

parts.label: Curved line
parts.note: A curving line means the slope keeps changing, so the object is speeding up or slowing down rather than moving at a steady speed.

parts.label: Tangent
parts.note: To read the speed at one instant on a curve, draw a tangent touching that point; its gradient gives the exact speed there.

parts.label: Velocity axis
parts.note: We plot how fast the object moves up this side, so higher up the graph means it is travelling faster.

parts.label: Time axis
parts.note: Time runs along the bottom, so reading left to right shows how the velocity changes as the seconds tick by.

parts.label: Gradient = acceleration
parts.note: The line's steepness tells us the acceleration: a steeper slope means velocity is changing faster each second, in metres per second squared.

parts.label: Area = distance
parts.note: Filling in the space beneath the line gives the distance travelled, since fast speeds over time cover more ground.

parts.label: Terminal velocity
parts.note: The line flattens out here: drag has grown to balance weight, the resultant force is zero, so it falls at steady speed.

parts.label: Deceleration
parts.note: When the line slopes downward the velocity is dropping, so the acceleration is negative and the object is slowing down.

parts.label: Trolley (mass)
parts.note: Here is our trolley with a set mass; we will push it and measure how quickly it speeds up along the track.

parts.label: Track
parts.note: The trolley runs along this smooth, level track, so we can watch its motion without friction hiding the effect of our force.

parts.label: Resultant force
parts.note: We pull the trolley with a resultant force; a bigger force makes it accelerate faster, since force equals mass times acceleration.

parts.label: Weight
parts.note: Gravity pulls the trolley down with its weight; on a level track this alone cannot change its forward motion.

parts.label: Normal (reaction) force
parts.note: The track pushes up with a normal force, exactly balancing the weight, so the trolley neither sinks nor lifts off.

parts.label: Acceleration
parts.note: The resultant force makes the trolley accelerate, gaining speed each second; double the force and the acceleration doubles too.

parts.label: Stopping distance
parts.note: The whole gap the car covers before it halts splits into two stretches: the thinking part plus the braking part added together.

parts.label: Thinking distance
parts.note: Before the brakes even touch, the car keeps rolling while the driver notices the hazard; tiredness, alcohol or distraction stretch this further.

parts.label: Braking distance
parts.note: Once the brakes bite, the car still travels forward as it slows; wet, icy roads or worn tyres lengthen this stretch.

parts.label: Driver reacts
parts.note: Here the driver spots the danger and decides to act, but their reaction time means the car has already moved on.

parts.label: Brakes applied
parts.note: Now the driver presses the pedal and the brakes start slowing the car, beginning the braking part of the journey.

parts.label: Braking wheel
parts.note: The brake grips the wheel, and a bigger braking force decelerates the car harder, though huge decelerations can be dangerous and overheat the brakes.

parts.label: Momentum (p = mv)
parts.note: The moving car carries momentum, mass times velocity; in a crash this total momentum is shared out but never lost overall.

parts.label: Cell
parts.note: The cell is the pump: it provides the potential difference that pushes electric charge round the whole circuit.

parts.label: Switch
parts.note: The switch is the gate: closed it lets charge flow, open it breaks the loop and everything stops.

parts.label: Ammeter (A)
parts.note: The ammeter sits in the line, in series, counting how much charge flows past each second, measured in amperes.

parts.label: Resistor
parts.note: The resistor squeezes the flow, opposing the charge and limiting how big the current can grow around the loop.

parts.label: Lamp
parts.note: Charge pushed through the lamp heats its thin filament until it glows, turning electrical energy into light.

parts.label: Closed loop
parts.note: Now the loop is complete with no breaks, so charge can flow all the way round and the lamp lights.

parts.label: Cell
parts.note: The cell pushes charge round the whole circuit, providing the potential difference that drives a current through the test wire.

parts.label: Ammeter
parts.note: Wired in series, the ammeter counts the current flowing through the wire in amps, one of your two key readings.

parts.label: Test wire
parts.note: Current squeezes along this wire; make it longer and it resists more, so the same voltage pushes a smaller current through.

parts.label: Voltmeter
parts.note: Connected in parallel across the wire, this reads the potential difference in volts, the energy given to each coulomb passing through.

parts.label: Connecting leads
parts.note: These low-resistance leads connect everything into one loop, so charge flows from cell, through wire and meters, and back.

parts.label: Resistor
parts.note: Push harder with more p.d. and the current climbs in step, so the I-V line stays perfectly straight through the origin.

parts.label: Filament lamp
parts.note: As current heats the thin wire, its resistance rises and chokes the flow, bending the line into an S-shaped curve.

parts.label: Diode
parts.note: Current pours through one way but hits a near-infinite wall the other way, so the graph only rises on one side.

parts.label: Thermistor
parts.note: Warm it up and its resistance drops, letting more current through, which lets circuits sense temperature and respond automatically.

parts.label: LDR
parts.note: Shine more light on it and its resistance falls, so current rises, letting a circuit detect brightness and switch things on.

parts.label: Test circuit (A & V)
parts.note: The ammeter counts current while the voltmeter reads p.d., so we can plot each component's I-V graph point by point.

parts.label: Battery (supply)
parts.note: The battery pushes charge out and drives the whole circuit; this potential difference is shared out to everything connected to it.

parts.label: Series loop
parts.note: Here the parts sit in one single loop, so the same current flows through every component, one after another, all the way round.

parts.label: Resistor
parts.note: Each resistor added to the loop squeezes the current more, so the total resistance grows and less current flows overall.

parts.label: Single break
parts.note: Snap the loop anywhere and the current has no path back, so everything switches off at once, like old fairy lights.

parts.label: Junction
parts.note: At this junction the current splits, giving it extra paths to flow through; more paths mean the total resistance actually drops.

parts.label: Parallel branch
parts.note: Each branch feels the full supply voltage; their separate currents rejoin, adding up to the total current leaving the battery.

parts.label: Cell
parts.note: The cell pushes charge round the circuit, driving the current that will deliver electrical power to the components.

parts.label: Potential difference
parts.note: The potential difference is the push per unit charge; multiply it by the current and you get the power transferred.

parts.label: Current
parts.note: Current is the flow of charge each second; a bigger current squared through resistance means more power delivered.

parts.label: Resistor
parts.note: Charge squeezing through the resistor transfers energy as heat; a higher power rating shifts that energy faster.

parts.label: Charge
parts.note: As each unit of charge crosses the potential difference, it hands over energy equal to charge times voltage.

parts.label: Energy transferred
parts.note: Energy pours out here as heat and light; the higher the power, the quicker this energy is transferred.

parts.label: Power station
parts.note: Here the journey begins: the power station generates alternating current, the back-and-forth mains electricity that will feed the whole grid.

parts.label: Step-up transformer
parts.note: Straight away the voltage is boosted right up. Raising the voltage drops the current flowing on into the transmission lines.

parts.label: Step-down transformer
parts.note: The low current wasted little heat along the cables, so now this transformer drops the voltage back down for safe use in homes.

parts.label: Live wire
parts.note: Inside the home cable, the brown live wire arrives carrying the full 230 V, delivering the energy that drives the appliance.

parts.label: Neutral wire
parts.note: The blue neutral wire sits near 0 V and carries the current back out, completing the circuit so charge keeps flowing.

parts.label: Earth wire
parts.note: The green-and-yellow earth wire stays quiet as a safety line, only carrying current if a fault sends charge astray.

parts.label: Fuse
parts.note: If too big a current flows in a fault, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit, cutting the danger off.

parts.label: North pole
parts.note: One end of the magnet is the north pole. Push another north near it and they repel, shoving apart without touching.

parts.label: South pole
parts.note: The other end is the south pole. A north and south pull towards each other, attracting across the gap as a non-contact force.

parts.label: Field line
parts.note: Now trace a field line looping out of the north pole and curving back into the south; where lines crowd together, the field is strongest.

parts.label: Plotting compass
parts.note: Drop a plotting compass in the field and its tiny magnet needle swings to line up, pointing along the field line's direction.

parts.label: Earth's field
parts.note: The Earth acts like one huge bar magnet inside, so its field tugs your compass needle round to point roughly north.

parts.label: Coil turns
parts.note: Winding the wire into a coil stacks each loop's field, adding them up into a strong, uniform field like a bar magnet's.

parts.label: Iron core
parts.note: Slotting an iron core inside concentrates the field, boosting the magnetism and letting you switch it on and off with the current.

parts.label: North pole
parts.note: The lined-up field bursts out one end as a north pole, giving the electromagnet a magnet's pulling power while the current flows.

parts.label: Battery (current)
parts.note: The battery pushes a current through the wire, and every moving current wraps a magnetic field around itself as it flows.

parts.label: Magnetic field
parts.note: Circular magnetic field lines curl around the wire; reverse the current and they flip direction, showing the field depends on current flow.

parts.label: North pole
parts.note: The north pole sends invisible field lines out into the gap, ready to push on any current flowing through the wire here.

parts.label: South pole
parts.note: The south pole pulls the field lines in, so the field runs straight across the gap from north to south.

parts.label: Magnetic field
parts.note: These lines mark the field crossing the gap; the wire sits at 90 degrees to them, giving the biggest possible push.

parts.label: Current-carrying coil
parts.note: Current flows along the wire through this field, and where the two meet a force is created that shoves the wire sideways.

parts.label: Upward force
parts.note: One side gets pushed up while the other is pushed down, so the coil turns, spinning the motor round.

parts.label: Split-ring commutator
parts.note: This split ring flips the current each half-turn, so the forces keep pushing the same way and the spin never stops.

parts.label: Battery
parts.note: The battery drives the current round the circuit and into the coil, powering the whole spinning motor.

parts.label: Sun (a star)
parts.note: We start with the Sun, our own star, sitting at the centre; its huge mass anchors everything else in the solar system.

parts.label: Planet
parts.note: Now a planet sweeps around the Sun, one of eight held in place as it travels its path through space.

parts.label: Moon (natural satellite)
parts.note: A moon circles the planet as its natural satellite, going round the planet the same way the planet goes round the Sun.

parts.label: Artificial satellite
parts.note: Here we launch an artificial satellite into orbit ourselves, sending it up to handle communications, weather-watching or GPS positioning.

parts.label: Gravity (pulls inward)
parts.note: Gravity now pulls inward on the satellite, and this constant tug is the force that curves its path into an orbit.

parts.label: Orbit
parts.note: The satellite settles into a stable orbit; at this radius one exact speed works, and closer orbits must travel faster.

parts.label: Nebula
parts.note: Here gravity slowly pulls a huge cloud of dust and gas together, tugging it inwards and squeezing it to start building a star.

parts.label: Protostar
parts.note: The squeezed gas heats up into a spinning protostar; once hot and dense enough, hydrogen nuclei begin to fuse and it starts to shine.

parts.label: Main sequence
parts.note: Now fusion pushes outwards while gravity pulls inwards; these forces balance, so the star holds a steady size for billions of years.

parts.label: Red giant
parts.note: As fuel runs low the balance tips, and a Sun-like star swells outwards, cooling its surface to red as it becomes a red giant.

parts.label: White dwarf
parts.note: The giant sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a small, hot, dense core called a white dwarf that gradually cools and fades.

parts.label: Supernova
parts.note: A far heavier star's core collapses and rebounds in a huge supernova explosion, scattering heavy elements beyond iron out into space.

parts.label: Black hole
parts.note: For the most massive stars, gravity crushes the leftover core so tightly that not even light can escape, forming a black hole.

parts.label: Big Bang
parts.note: It all starts here: the universe erupts from a tiny, hot, dense point and has been expanding outward ever since.

parts.label: Distant galaxy
parts.note: This galaxy sits far out in space, and being furthest away it races away from us the fastest.

parts.label: Nearer galaxy
parts.note: A closer galaxy is still fleeing, but being nearer it moves away more slowly than the distant one.

parts.label: Moving apart
parts.note: Space itself stretches, carrying every galaxy apart from every other, like dots on an inflating balloon.

parts.label: Source light
parts.note: Each galaxy sends out light with its own wavelengths, our starting ruler before the journey across expanding space.

parts.label: Red-shifted light
parts.note: As the galaxy speeds away, its light gets stretched to longer wavelengths, shifting towards red and proving the universe expands.

parts.label: Transverse wave
parts.note: Watch the wave travel sideways while the particles bob up and down at right angles to it, carrying energy along without moving matter.

parts.label: Amplitude
parts.note: Measure from the rest line up to the crest: the bigger this height, the more energy the wave carries as it travels.

parts.label: Wavelength
parts.note: Measure from one crest across to the next crest: that gap is one complete wave repeating over and over as it moves.

parts.label: Longitudinal wave
parts.note: Now the particles jiggle back and forth along the same direction the wave travels, squashing and stretching as sound does through air.

parts.label: Compression
parts.note: Here the particles bunch up tightly, squeezing together as the wave pushes through and momentarily raising the pressure.

parts.label: Rarefaction
parts.note: Here the particles spread far apart, stretched thin between compressions, lowering the pressure before the next squeeze arrives.

parts.label: Crest
parts.note: Here's the top of the wave, its highest point. Count how many crests pass each second and you have the frequency.

parts.label: Trough
parts.note: The wave dips to its lowest point here. A crest plus a trough makes one full wave carrying energy along.

parts.label: Wavelength
parts.note: Measure crest-to-crest and you have the wavelength. Multiply it by frequency and you get how fast the wave travels.

parts.label: Amplitude
parts.note: Measured from rest to the crest, this shows how much energy the wave carries, though it never changes the wave speed.

parts.label: Rest Position
parts.note: This is where the water or string sits still. The wave makes it wobble up and down about this line as energy passes.

parts.label: Ripple Tank
parts.note: Send ripples across shallow water here, then time and measure them to work out the wave speed for real.

parts.label: Electromagnetic spectrum
parts.note: Here is the whole family of electromagnetic waves laid out in a band; every one is a transverse wave racing through vacuum at the speed of light.

parts.label: Radio waves
parts.note: At this end sit radio waves, the lowest frequency and longest wavelength members, where the spectrum begins before frequency climbs across the band.

parts.label: Gamma rays
parts.note: At the far end come gamma rays, the highest frequency and shortest wavelength waves, showing how far frequency rises across the spectrum.

parts.label: Transverse wave
parts.note: Each wave wobbles up and down at right angles to its direction of travel, marking every member of this family as transverse.

parts.label: Increasing wavelength
parts.note: Reading this way the waves stretch out longer, so wavelength grows towards the radio end while frequency drops the same direction.

parts.label: Increasing frequency
parts.note: Reading the other way the waves pack tighter, so frequency climbs towards gamma rays even though the speed in vacuum never changes.

parts.label: Refraction at a boundary
parts.note: Crossing a boundary the wave changes speed, and meeting it at an angle bends the ray as the change of speed refracts it.

parts.label: Radio waves
parts.note: We start at the low-frequency end: radio waves carry TV and radio broadcasts through the air to aerials in your home.

parts.label: Infrared
parts.note: Further along, infrared carries heat. Black matt surfaces pour it out best, so warm objects glow strongly in the infrared.

parts.label: Ultraviolet
parts.note: Push higher and waves turn harmful: ultraviolet packs enough energy to damage skin cells, causing sunburn and, over time, skin cancer.

parts.label: X-rays & gamma
parts.note: At the top sit X-rays and gamma rays. These ionise atoms, tearing at cells and DNA, so exposure can trigger cancer.

parts.label: Increasing frequency
parts.note: This arrow tracks frequency climbing left to right; as it rises the waves carry more energy and grow more dangerous.

parts.label: Leslie cube
parts.note: The Leslie cube tests this: fill it with hot water and each face radiates infrared, letting us compare surfaces fairly.

parts.label: Black matt face
parts.note: Point the detector here and the reading spikes: the black matt face emits far more infrared than the cube's shiny sides.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: Inside the nucleus the genetic information is stored; when a sperm's 23 chromosomes join an ovum's 23, the zygote gets a full set of 46.

parts.label: Chromosome
parts.note: Zooming in, we see one chromosome; your body cells each pack 46 of these thread-like structures, arranged neatly into 23 matching pairs.

parts.label: Chromosome Pair
parts.note: The two chromosomes pair up because one came from your mother and one from your father, so each parent contributes half your instructions.

parts.label: Double Helix
parts.note: Unwinding a chromosome reveals DNA: a long molecule twisted into a double helix, like a ladder spiralled round, holding all the code.

parts.label: DNA Base Pair
parts.note: The ladder's rungs are pairs of bases; their exact order along the strand spells out the coded instructions the cell reads.

parts.label: Gene
parts.note: A short stretch of this base sequence is one gene, carrying the code to build a single protein; each chromosome holds many genes.

parts.label: Incident ray
parts.note: This is the incoming beam of light travelling in a straight line towards the surface, ready to hit it and be reflected.

parts.label: Normal
parts.note: This dashed line sits at right angles to the mirror; we measure both angles from it to compare them fairly.

parts.label: Reflected ray
parts.note: The light bounces off and heads away in a new straight line; if it reaches your eye, you see the object.

parts.label: Mirror
parts.note: The smooth shiny surface reflects nearly all the light back rather than absorbing or letting it pass through.

parts.label: Refracted ray
parts.note: Entering the glass, the light slows down and bends, so its path kinks towards the normal as it crosses over.

parts.label: Prism
parts.note: The angled glass block refracts the white light, bending each colour by a slightly different amount as it passes through.

parts.label: Spectrum
parts.note: The colours fan out and emerge separated as red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet, revealing white light's hidden mix.

parts.label: Metal + acid
parts.note: Drop a metal into acid and it fizzes: the acid attacks it, giving a salt plus hydrogen gas that streams off as bubbles.

parts.label: Reactivity series
parts.note: Some metals fizz furiously, others barely react, so we rank them by how vigorously they react into a league table of reactivity.

parts.label: Furnace
parts.note: In the furnace we heat the metal's ore with carbon; the carbon grabs the oxygen away, freeing the pure metal like iron.

parts.label: Ceramic
parts.note: Heating wet clay drives off the water, so the molecules can no longer slide past each other, setting hard and brittle.

parts.label: Polymer chain
parts.note: Many small monomers join into one long chain; where chains slide over each other you get a plastic that stretches and melts.

parts.label: Composite
parts.note: Combine flexible steel bars with strong concrete and the composite gains both: it bends without snapping yet resists being crushed.

parts.label: Atmosphere
parts.note: Up here the air is thin, so less weight of air pushes down and atmospheric pressure is low; it climbs as you descend.

parts.label: Fluid (water)
parts.note: Below the air sits water, a fluid that flows and presses on anything inside it as its particles collide with surfaces.

parts.label: Floating object
parts.note: The boat is spread into a wide hull, touching lots of water, so more upthrust pushes up and it stays afloat.

parts.label: Weight
parts.note: Gravity pulls the boat straight down with its weight, the downward force the water must somehow match to stop it sinking.

parts.label: Upthrust
parts.note: The water pushes back up with an upthrust; here it exactly equals the weight, so forces balance and the boat floats.

parts.label: Pressure with depth
parts.note: Go deeper and the arrows grow longer: more water weighs down from above, so the pressure pushing outwards keeps increasing.

parts.label: Filter funnel
parts.note: We pour the muddy mixture in here; the filter paper acts as a sieve, letting the liquid slip through but stopping the solid.

parts.label: Residue
parts.note: The insoluble solid can't fit through the tiny holes, so it stays trapped on the paper as the leftover residue.

parts.label: Filtrate
parts.note: The clear liquid drips through the paper into the beaker below; this collected liquid is called the filtrate.

parts.label: Solute
parts.note: This is the solid we stir in to dissolve; its particles don't vanish, they spread out and hide between the liquid particles.

parts.label: Solvent
parts.note: This is the liquid doing the dissolving; its particles make room so the solute spreads through and forms a clear solution.

parts.label: Crystals
parts.note: As the solvent boils away into the air, the dissolved solute is left behind, growing back into solid crystals.

parts.label: Evaporating dish
parts.note: We heat the solution in this shallow dish; its wide surface lets the solvent evaporate quickly, leaving the solute behind.

parts.label: Device
parts.note: Here is our device, doing a job. As it works it transfers energy from its supply out into the world every second.

parts.label: Energy supply
parts.note: Energy flows in from the supply to feed the device. Without this store of energy, the device has nothing to transfer.

parts.label: Energy transferred
parts.note: Energy pours through in joules. Power will measure how fast this flow moves, not just the total amount transferred.

parts.label: Power rating
parts.note: The power rating in watts tells us the speed: 1 watt means 1 joule is transferred every single second.

parts.label: Time
parts.note: The clock times how long energy is transferred. We convert to seconds first, multiplying any minutes by 60.

parts.label: P = E ÷ t
parts.note: Divide the energy transferred by the time taken and out pops the power: P = E ÷ t.

parts.label: Glucose
parts.note: Glucose is the fuel going in; its chemical bonds hold the energy the cell is about to release, not burn as breathing.

parts.label: Oxygen
parts.note: Oxygen joins the glucose, breathed in through the lungs and delivered by blood, so the fuel can be broken down fully.

parts.label: Mitochondria
parts.note: Inside these tiny structures the glucose and oxygen react, making mitochondria the power stations where energy is actually released.

parts.label: Cell
parts.note: Everything happens inside the living cell, where digested glucose and breathed-in oxygen arrive together to keep the cell alive.

parts.label: CO₂ + Water
parts.note: Carbon dioxide and water leave as waste; they are breathed out and removed once the energy has been released from glucose.

parts.label: Lactic Acid
parts.note: Without enough oxygen, human cells break glucose only into lactic acid, releasing far less energy and making muscles ache.

parts.label: Fermentation
parts.note: In yeast the oxygen-free route splits glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, the reaction that makes bread rise and brews alcohol.

parts.label: Transverse wave
parts.note: We start by drawing the wave that carries the energy along; here the wobble is up-and-down, across the direction it travels.

parts.label: Wavelength
parts.note: One full ripple, crest to crest, is the wavelength; squeeze more ripples per second and the pitch you hear climbs higher.

parts.label: Amplitude
parts.note: How tall the wave rises measures the amplitude; the bigger this swing, the more energy carried, so the louder the sound.

parts.label: Vibrating source
parts.note: Every sound begins here as something vibrates back and forth, shaking whatever surrounds it and starting the wave off.

parts.label: Air particles (medium)
parts.note: The vibrating source pushes the air particles, making them oscillate and knock into neighbours, passing energy along without travelling themselves.

parts.label: Compression
parts.note: As particles bunch up they form a compression, a squeezed patch that moves outward, carrying the sound energy through the air.

parts.label: Ear drum / diaphragm
parts.note: Finally the wave hits your ear drum, or a microphone's diaphragm, making it vibrate so the sound gets detected.

parts.label: Sun (a star)
parts.note: It all starts here: the Sun, a giant ball of glowing gas, sits at the centre while eight planets circle around it.

parts.label: Orbit
parts.note: Each planet travels this looping path, held in place by the Sun's gravity constantly pulling it inwards so it never flies off into space.

parts.label: Rocky planet
parts.note: Closest to the Sun sit the four rocky planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — small worlds with solid, stony surfaces you could stand on.

parts.label: Moon
parts.note: Some planets have moons, which loop around the planet the same way the planet loops the Sun, tugged along by the planet's gravity.

parts.label: Gas planet
parts.note: Further out sit the giant gas planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — huge worlds with no solid ground, just thick swirling gas.

parts.label: Galaxy (Milky Way)
parts.note: Zoom right out and our whole Solar System is one tiny speck in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy holding billions of stars.

parts.label: Tilted axis
parts.note: Earth spins around this tilted line once a day, turning us towards the Sun for daytime and away into darkness for night.

parts.label: Proton (+)
parts.note: Deep inside every atom sit positive protons; normally equal numbers of electrons balance them, so the whole material starts with no charge.

parts.label: Positively Charged Object
parts.note: This object has lost some electrons to the cloth, leaving more protons than electrons, so it now carries an overall positive charge.

parts.label: Rubbing Cloth
parts.note: As the cloth rubs the insulator, friction drags electrons across the surface, moving negative charge from one material to the other.

parts.label: Negatively Charged Object
parts.note: The cloth's electrons pile up here, giving this object extra negative charge, so it now attracts the opposite positive object nearby.

parts.label: Field Lines
parts.note: Field lines map the space around the charges where forces act; packed tightly they show a strong field, spread out they show a weaker one.

parts.label: Field Line Arrow
parts.note: Each arrow shows which way a positive charge would be pushed: away from the positive object and towards the negative one.

parts.label: Electric Field
parts.note: The whole field region lets the charges push and pull each other without touching, exerting an electrostatic force across empty space.

parts.label: Classification
parts.note: We begin by sorting living things into groups by their features, called classification, using the system Carl Linnaeus built to make sense of nature.

parts.label: Five Kingdoms
parts.note: The biggest sort splits every organism into five kingdoms, so a bacterium and an oak tree land in completely different branches.

parts.label: Vertebrate
parts.note: Zoom into animals and we split again: vertebrates have a backbone running down them, giving support and protecting the nerve cord inside.

parts.label: Invertebrate
parts.note: Everything without a backbone, like insects and worms, drops into invertebrates, the far larger group making up most animal species.

parts.label: Species
parts.note: The smallest group is a species: two organisms belong together only if they can breed and produce fertile offspring that can breed too.

parts.label: Conservation
parts.note: When species start disappearing we step in with conservation, protecting habitats and running breeding programmes to keep biodiversity high.

parts.label: Seed Vault
parts.note: As a backup, a global seed vault freezes millions of seeds, so if disease wipes out a crop we can regrow it.

parts.label: Reactants
parts.note: We start on the left with the reactants — the starting substances whose atoms are about to be rearranged into something new.

parts.label: Reaction arrow
parts.note: The arrow means 'turns into', not equals — it shows the reactants changing one way into fresh products, never back again.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: On the right we get the products: brand-new substances built from the same atoms, but now with different properties.

parts.label: Combustion
parts.note: In combustion a fuel burns in oxygen, releasing energy and usually giving out carbon dioxide and water as products.

parts.label: Thermal decomposition
parts.note: Here heat alone splits one reactant apart — a metal carbonate breaks into a metal oxide plus carbon dioxide gas.

parts.label: Oxidation (rust)
parts.note: In oxidation an element grabs oxygen — iron slowly joins with oxygen to form iron oxide, which we see as rust.

parts.label: Signs of reaction
parts.note: Watch for the tell-tale signs a reaction is happening: heat change, light, colour change, fizzing, or a solid precipitate appearing.

parts.label: Mass conserved
parts.note: No atoms vanish — they're only rearranged, so the products always weigh exactly the same as the reactants did.

parts.label: Solid (densest)
parts.note: Here the particles are jammed tightly together with little space between them, so the most mass fits in the smallest volume, making solids densest.

parts.label: Liquid
parts.note: Now the particles have loosened and can slide past each other, spreading out a little, so a liquid is usually less dense than its solid.

parts.label: Gas (least dense)
parts.note: Here the particles fly far apart into the empty space, so very little mass fills a big volume, making a gas the least dense state.

parts.label: Water surface
parts.note: At the water surface the particles are constantly jiggling and moving randomly, Brownian motion, proving the particles inside are never truly still.

parts.label: Floating ice
parts.note: Water is odd: its solid packs less tightly than the liquid, so ice is less dense than water and floats on top.

parts.label: Denser object sinks
parts.note: This object is denser than the water around it, so it cannot stay up and sinks straight to the bottom.

parts.label: Carbohydrates
parts.note: We start the plate with carbohydrates, the fuel that gives your body most of its energy for moving, thinking and staying warm.

parts.label: Protein
parts.note: Next we add protein, which the body uses to grow new cells and repair damaged ones, like building blocks for your muscles.

parts.label: Fats
parts.note: A small slice of fats goes on to insulate and cushion your organs, though too much on the plate can harm your health.

parts.label: Fibre
parts.note: Fibre joins the plate to keep food moving through your gut, preventing constipation and keeping digestion healthy.

parts.label: Vitamins & Minerals
parts.note: Vitamins and minerals fill the last slice: calcium builds bones, iron helps blood carry oxygen, and vitamins protect eyesight and immunity.

parts.label: Balanced Plate
parts.note: Together these slices make a balanced plate, since no single food holds all seven nutrients, we must eat a variety.

parts.label: Water
parts.note: Finally we pour water over everything, letting chemical reactions happen inside cells and carrying substances around your whole body.

parts.label: Atmosphere
parts.note: A thin blanket of gas wraps the planet: mostly nitrogen, about a fifth oxygen for breathing, plus tiny traces like carbon dioxide.

parts.label: Crust
parts.note: This is the thin rocky skin we live on, only tens of kilometres deep, floating on the hotter layers pressing up beneath it.

parts.label: Mantle
parts.note: Beneath the crust sits the vast, slowly flowing mantle, whose heat drives movement in the rock above it.

parts.label: Outer core
parts.note: Deeper still, iron here is so hot it melts into molten liquid, churning around the solid centre below.

parts.label: Inner core
parts.note: At the very centre the pressure squeezes the iron so hard it stays solid, forming the planet's hot inner heart.

parts.label: Element
parts.note: We start with an element: a pure substance built from only one type of atom, like the copper in a wire or oxygen gas.

parts.label: Compound
parts.note: Now join different atoms together with chemical bonds and you make a compound, a brand-new substance holding two or more types of atom.

parts.label: Mixture
parts.note: In a mixture the substances just sit together, not bonded, so you can pull them apart again, like lifting iron filings out of sulfur with a magnet.

parts.label: Chemical bond
parts.note: The chemical bond is the glue: it locks different atoms together so tightly they now behave as one whole new substance, not a mixture.

parts.label: Molecule (formula)
parts.note: We write the result as a formula, using symbols and small numbers to count each atom, so H₂O tells us two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen.

parts.label: New properties
parts.note: Bonding transforms everything: soft sodium metal and toxic chlorine gas combine to give ordinary table salt, with completely new properties of its own.

parts.label: Exothermic
parts.note: In an exothermic change, energy pours out of the reaction into everything around it, so the surroundings warm up.

parts.label: Energy out
parts.note: Energy escapes to the surroundings here, just like a hand warmer or self-heating can pushing out heat when it reacts.

parts.label: Endothermic
parts.note: In an endothermic change, the reaction pulls energy in from around it, so the surroundings cool down instead.

parts.label: Energy in
parts.note: Energy is dragged in from the surroundings here, the way an instant icepack sucks heat away and turns cold.

parts.label: Thermometer
parts.note: The thermometer reads the temperature: if it rises the change is exothermic, if it falls it is endothermic.

parts.label: Surroundings
parts.note: The surroundings include the thermometer itself, which is exactly why it can sense the energy moving in or out.

parts.label: Fossil fuel
parts.note: Coal, oil or gas arrives first, packed with stored energy from living things that died millions of years ago.

parts.label: Boiler / steam
parts.note: The fuel is burned to heat water in the boiler until it boils, and the hot steam rushes out to spin the turbine.

parts.label: Turbine
parts.note: The fast-moving steam pushes the turbine blades round, so this spinning is what every power station really needs.

parts.label: Generator
parts.note: The spinning turbine turns the generator, and it is here that the movement is converted into an electric current.

parts.label: Dam (hydro)
parts.note: A hydro station skips burning fuel: water released from behind the dam rushes down and spins the same turbine instead.

parts.label: National Grid
parts.note: The current flows out along the National Grid's cables, carrying electricity to homes, businesses and factories everywhere.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: At the centre sits a tiny nucleus — only a ten-thousandth of the atom's width, yet it packs in almost all the mass.

parts.label: Proton
parts.note: Inside the nucleus we pack positive protons; how many there are decides which element this atom actually is.

parts.label: Neutron
parts.note: Alongside them sit neutral neutrons, adding mass but no charge, helping bind the crowded nucleus together.

parts.label: Electron
parts.note: Now tiny negative electrons appear, far lighter than protons, whizzing around the nucleus in the mostly empty space.

parts.label: Electron shell
parts.note: The electrons settle into shells — energy levels at set distances — filling from the innermost outwards around the nucleus.

parts.label: Ejected electron (ion)
parts.note: Absorbing electromagnetic radiation can knock an electron clean out, leaving the atom with extra positive charge — now a positive ion.

parts.label: Alpha source
parts.note: Here we fire a beam of tiny positive alpha particles at the foil, testing whether Thomson's soft plum-pudding atom really holds up.

parts.label: Gold foil
parts.note: The beam hits gold hammered incredibly thin, just a few atoms deep, so we can watch how each particle passes through the atoms.

parts.label: Passes straight through
parts.note: Almost every particle sails straight through undeflected, telling us the atom is mostly empty space with nothing solid in the way.

parts.label: Deflected / bounced back
parts.note: A few particles swerve sharply or bounce right back, so something tiny, dense and positive must be repelling them.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: That something is the nucleus: a minuscule, dense, positively charged core at the centre where nearly all the atom's mass is packed.

parts.label: Electron shell
parts.note: Bohr adds electrons orbiting the nucleus at fixed distances in shells, each shell a set energy level rather than a random cloud.

parts.label: Neutron
parts.note: Finally Chadwick finds neutrons sitting in the nucleus, uncharged particles that add mass and complete our picture of the atom.

parts.label: Alpha particle
parts.note: An unstable nucleus flings out an alpha particle, a heavy clump of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, losing energy as it decays.

parts.label: Beta particle
parts.note: Instead a fast-moving electron shoots out of the nucleus, carrying energy away much lighter and quicker than an alpha particle.

parts.label: Gamma ray
parts.note: The nucleus also releases a burst of pure electromagnetic energy, a gamma ray, needing no particle to carry it away.

parts.label: Neutron
parts.note: Sometimes a lone neutron is thrown out of the nucleus, a neutral particle with no charge to attract or repel it.

parts.label: Paper
parts.note: The heavy alpha barely gets anywhere: a single sheet of paper absorbs it completely, blocking its path here.

parts.label: Aluminium
parts.note: Beta pushes further, but a few millimetres of aluminium soak it up, stopping the electrons dead.

parts.label: Lead / concrete
parts.note: Gamma streaks through almost everything; only thick lead or concrete can absorb enough to weaken the beam.

parts.label: Geiger-Muller tube
parts.note: A Geiger-Muller tube catches each particle as it arrives, clicking out a count-rate that reveals the source's activity in becquerel.

parts.label: Parent nucleus
parts.note: We start with an unstable parent nucleus, packed with too many protons and neutrons, so it is about to break apart to become more stable.

parts.label: Alpha particle
parts.note: The nucleus flings out an alpha particle of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, dropping its mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.

parts.label: Beta particle (electron)
parts.note: In beta decay a neutron flips into a proton and fires out a fast electron, so the atomic number climbs by 1 while mass stays the same.

parts.label: Activity curve
parts.note: As nuclei decay, the count-rate drops, tracing this falling curve; the time for the activity to halve is one half-life.

parts.label: After 1 half-life
parts.note: After one half-life, half the unstable nuclei have decayed, so the activity has dropped to exactly half its starting value.

parts.label: After 2 half-lives
parts.note: After a second half-life, the activity halves again, leaving just a quarter of the original count-rate on the curve.

parts.label: External source
parts.note: The story starts here: a radioactive source sits outside the body, firing radiation across the gap without ever touching you.

parts.label: Radiation rays
parts.note: The rays stream from the source and pass through the body from outside; this exposure is irradiation, but no radioactive atoms are left behind.

parts.label: Contaminant on body
parts.note: Now radioactive atoms land on the body itself; unlike irradiation, this source sticks around and keeps firing radiation from where it clings.

parts.label: Exposed body
parts.note: The exposed body absorbs the incoming radiation, but once the external source is removed the person is no longer radioactive.

parts.label: Shield (precaution)
parts.note: Slide a dense shield between source and body and it blocks most rays, cutting your dose alongside keeping distance and limiting time.

parts.label: Background source
parts.note: All around, low-level background radiation drips in constantly from radon, rocks, soil, space and food, the baseline dose we all receive.

parts.label: Cell wall
parts.note: A tough cellulose wall builds around the plant cell, giving it a rigid shape and stopping it bursting when it fills with water.

parts.label: Cell membrane
parts.note: Just inside sits the thin membrane, controlling what enters and leaves so useful substances get in and waste passes out.

parts.label: Chloroplast
parts.note: Green chloroplasts, packed with chlorophyll, trap sunlight energy to make food for the plant in photosynthesis.

parts.label: Mitochondria
parts.note: Tiny mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing the energy the cell needs to power everything it does.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: The nucleus sits in the centre, holding the DNA instructions and acting as the control room directing all the cell's activities.

parts.label: Cytoplasm
parts.note: Jelly-like cytoplasm fills the cell, a watery space where the chemical reactions of life keep happening.

parts.label: Ribosomes
parts.note: Scattered through the cytoplasm, tiny ribosomes read the instructions and build the proteins the cell needs to work.

parts.label: Eyepiece lens
parts.note: You look through the eyepiece lens first; it magnifies the image again, so total magnification equals eyepiece times objective magnification.

parts.label: Objective lens
parts.note: The objective lens sits close to the specimen and does the first magnifying, gathering light to enlarge the tiny object before the eyepiece.

parts.label: Specialised cell
parts.note: Under magnification you see a specialised cell: it differentiated from a general cell, gaining features that let it do one particular job well.

parts.label: Root hair cell
parts.note: This root hair cell grew a long projection, giving a huge surface area so water and minerals are absorbed faster from the soil.

parts.label: Stem cell
parts.note: A stem cell stays unspecialised, dividing and differentiating into any needed cell type, supplying replacements from embryos, bone marrow or plant meristems.

parts.label: Partially permeable membrane
parts.note: This barrier lets some particles through but not others, so it controls what enters and leaves the cell.

parts.label: Diffusion
parts.note: Particles spread out on their own, moving from where they are crowded to where they are sparse, needing no energy.

parts.label: Osmosis (water)
parts.note: Water slips across the membrane towards the more concentrated side, evening out the solution without any energy used.

parts.label: Active transport
parts.note: Here substances are pumped uphill against the gradient, so the cell must spend energy from respiration to do it.

parts.label: Mitosis
parts.note: The cell copies its DNA then splits, producing two identical cells to grow the organism or repair damaged tissue.

parts.label: Concentration gradient
parts.note: A steeper drop in concentration, more surface area and a shorter path all speed up how fast particles diffuse across.

parts.label: Light energy
parts.note: Light energy pours in from the Sun, powering the whole reaction — without it, nothing else can start.

parts.label: Chlorophyll
parts.note: The green pigment chlorophyll traps that light energy, capturing it so the leaf can drive the reaction forward.

parts.label: Leaf
parts.note: Inside the leaf's cells, the trapped energy joins the raw materials together, turning them into glucose and oxygen.

parts.label: Carbon dioxide in
parts.note: Carbon dioxide seeps in through tiny holes in the leaf, supplying the carbon needed to build glucose.

parts.label: Water from roots
parts.note: Water is pulled up from the roots into the leaf, providing the hydrogen that helps form the glucose.

parts.label: Oxygen out
parts.note: Oxygen is made as a waste product and escapes out through the leaf's holes into the air around it.

parts.label: Starch store
parts.note: Spare glucose is packed away as starch, storing the trapped energy for the plant to use later.

parts.label: Glucose
parts.note: Glucose is the fuel: this sugar carries the stored energy that respiration will unlock, feeding into every living cell nonstop.

parts.label: Oxygen in
parts.note: Oxygen is breathed in and delivered to the cell, where it will react with the glucose to release far more energy.

parts.label: Living cell
parts.note: Inside every living cell the glucose and oxygen meet and react, running the exothermic reaction that powers the whole organism.

parts.label: CO₂ + water
parts.note: The reaction makes carbon dioxide and water as waste; these leave the cell to be breathed out and removed by the blood.

parts.label: Energy released
parts.note: The real prize: energy is released for movement, growth and warmth, driving all the cell's other reactions.

parts.label: Lactic acid
parts.note: Without enough oxygen the muscle switches to anaerobic respiration, releasing less energy and building up lactic acid that makes muscles ache.

parts.label: Receptor
parts.note: It all starts here: the receptor detects a change (the stimulus), like heat or pressure, and fires off a tiny electrical impulse.

parts.label: Sensory neurone
parts.note: The sensory neurone carries that impulse away from the receptor, racing it inwards towards the spinal cord to report what was detected.

parts.label: Coordination centre
parts.note: The spinal cord receives the incoming signal and decides on a response, coordinating what happens next without waiting for the conscious brain.

parts.label: Synapse
parts.note: The neurones don't quite touch: a chemical squirts across this tiny gap and triggers a fresh impulse in the next neurone.

parts.label: Motor neurone
parts.note: The motor neurone now carries the outgoing command back out from the spinal cord, heading straight for the muscle that must act.

parts.label: Effector (muscle)
parts.note: The message arrives and the effector responds: the muscle contracts, pulling you away fast to protect the body from harm.

parts.label: Pituitary gland
parts.note: Sitting in the brain, this master gland fires out FSH and LH that travel down to switch other glands like the ovaries on.

parts.label: Thyroid gland
parts.note: Here in the neck, this gland drips its hormone straight into passing blood, giving a slow, steady message rather than a quick nerve zap.

parts.label: Liver
parts.note: When insulin arrives, the liver mops up spare glucose from the blood and locks it away as glycogen, dropping blood sugar back down.

parts.label: Pancreas
parts.note: This gland senses blood glucose climbing too high and releases insulin, the chemical signal telling the body to store the extra sugar.

parts.label: Hormone in blood
parts.note: The released hormone rides the bloodstream to every organ, but only its target organ recognises it and responds to the message.

parts.label: Ovaries
parts.note: Once the pituitary signals them, the ovaries pump out oestrogen, the main female hormone that drives the menstrual cycle each month.

parts.label: Pathogen types
parts.note: Meet the culprits: tiny microorganisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists — that invade the body and cause communicable diseases you can catch from others.

parts.label: Host cell
parts.note: Here's one of your body cells, working normally — but it's about to be hijacked by a pathogen that needs it to survive.

parts.label: Virus
parts.note: The virus slips inside the cell and forces it to make copies of the virus, damaging the cell as new viruses burst out.

parts.label: Droplet (air)
parts.note: When someone coughs or sneezes, pathogens ride tiny droplets through the air, ready to be breathed in by the next person.

parts.label: Vector
parts.note: A vector like a mosquito carries the pathogen from person to person, injecting malaria protists into the blood as it bites.

parts.label: Vaccination
parts.note: A vaccine trains the body to recognise the pathogen in advance, so far fewer people catch it and the spread is stopped.

parts.label: Skin barrier
parts.note: First line of defence: the skin forms a tough physical wall that stops most pathogens ever getting inside the body.

parts.label: Mucus & cilia
parts.note: In the airways, sticky mucus traps pathogens and tiny hair-like cilia sweep the trapped mucus back up and out.

parts.label: Stomach acid
parts.note: Any pathogens swallowed down are met by strong stomach acid, which kills them before they can invade the gut.

parts.label: White blood cell
parts.note: If pathogens slip past, white blood cells hunt them down and engulf them in phagocytosis, swallowing them whole.

parts.label: Pathogen
parts.note: This invading pathogen carries unique markers, triggering white blood cells to make matching antibodies and antitoxins against it.

parts.label: Antibiotic vs bacteria
parts.note: Antibiotics kill bacteria inside the body, but not viruses; overusing them breeds resistant strains like MRSA that survive.

parts.label: Drug trial test
parts.note: New drugs are trialled for safety, correct dose and effectiveness, using placebos and double-blind tests before approval.

parts.label: Enzyme
parts.note: Here comes the enzyme, a protein that speeds up a reaction and then walks away unchanged, ready to do it all again.

parts.label: Active site
parts.note: This notch is the active site, a shape that fits just one substrate like a key fits one lock, so only the right molecule slots in.

parts.label: Substrate
parts.note: The substrate drops into the active site; held snugly in place, its bonds are put under strain and made easier to break.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: The bonds snap and the products fall away, like starch cut into sugars, freeing the enzyme to grab the next substrate.

parts.label: Denatured enzyme
parts.note: Too much heat or the wrong pH warps the active site; now the substrate no longer fits, so the reaction grinds to a halt.

parts.label: Lungs
parts.note: Blood is pumped to the lungs first, picking up oxygen and dropping off waste carbon dioxide before returning to the heart.

parts.label: Artery
parts.note: This artery carries oxygen-rich blood away from the heart, its thick muscular walls withstanding the high pressure of each pump.

parts.label: Vein
parts.note: This vein returns blood to the heart at low pressure; its valves stop the slow-moving blood from flowing backwards.

parts.label: Heart
parts.note: The heart sits at the centre, pumping blood twice: once out to the lungs and once out around the whole body.

parts.label: Coronary artery
parts.note: Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle itself; if fatty deposits narrow them, the starved muscle causes coronary heart disease.

parts.label: Body tissues
parts.note: At the body tissues, blood delivers oxygen and collects waste, then heads back to the heart to be pumped round again.

parts.label: Capillary
parts.note: Here blood slows through tiny capillaries whose walls are one cell thick, letting oxygen and food pass into the tissues.

parts.label: Blood components
parts.note: The blood itself carries red cells for oxygen, white cells to fight pathogens, platelets to clot, and plasma dissolving everything else.

parts.label: Leaf
