parts.note: Start at the leaf, the plant's food factory: it traps sunlight for photosynthesis and is where the water journey ends.

parts.label: Stem
parts.note: The stem holds the plant up and forms the highway between roots and leaves, carrying water up and sugars back down.

parts.label: Roots
parts.note: Roots anchor the plant and soak up water and dissolved minerals from the soil, feeding them into the transport system.

parts.label: Xylem
parts.note: Xylem pipes, made of dead hollow cells, carry water and minerals one way: upwards from the roots to the thirsty leaves.

parts.label: Phloem
parts.note: Living phloem tubes flow the other way, carrying sugars made in the leaves out to growing roots and stems (translocation).

parts.label: Stomata
parts.note: Tiny stomata on the leaf underside open to let water vapour escape, releasing water lost through the leaf surface.

parts.label: Transpiration stream
parts.note: As water evaporates out, it drags more water up the xylem behind it: this continuous pull is the transpiration stream.

parts.label: Egg (gamete)
parts.note: The mother makes an egg, a sex cell carrying just half her genetic information, waiting to be joined by the other parent.

parts.label: Sperm (gamete)
parts.note: The father's sperm swims in carrying his half of the genes, ready to fuse with the egg and mix two sets of information.

parts.label: Fertilised cell
parts.note: Egg and sperm fuse at fertilisation, restoring the full set of chromosomes; this single cell now divides by mitosis to grow.

parts.label: Single parent (clone)
parts.note: With no gametes and no mixing, one parent simply copies itself, so every offspring is an identical clone with no variation.

parts.label: Chromosomes (halved)
parts.note: Meiosis halves the chromosomes when making gametes, so two joining cells add back to the normal number rather than doubling it.

parts.label: DNA double helix
parts.note: Zoom into a chromosome and you find DNA: two long strands twisted together into a double helix that stores all the instructions.

parts.label: Gene / base pair
parts.note: The strands are held by paired bases; a short run of these forms one gene, coding for a single feature of the organism.

parts.label: Parent alleles
parts.note: Each parent carries two alleles for the gene; here both are Bb, so each can pass on either a B or a b to their offspring.

parts.label: Dominant offspring
parts.note: Where a dominant B lands in the square, it overrides the other allele, so the offspring shows the dominant characteristic even with just one copy.

parts.label: Heterozygous (Bb)
parts.note: A B pairs with a b, giving two different alleles; the dominant B is expressed, so the phenotype still shows the dominant characteristic.

parts.label: Recessive (bb)
parts.note: Only when two recessive b alleles meet does the recessive characteristic finally appear, since no dominant allele is present to mask it.

parts.label: 3 : 1 ratio
parts.note: Counting the four squares gives three offspring showing dominant to one showing recessive, the classic 3:1 ratio from two heterozygous parents.

parts.label: XX / XY sex
parts.note: Sex is set the same way: an X from mum pairs with an X or Y from dad, giving XX females or XY males.

parts.label: Varied population
parts.note: We start with a population where individuals differ — their genes, environment, or both make no two exactly alike, giving natural selection something to act on.

parts.label: Mutation / new allele
parts.note: A random mutation copies a gene wrongly, creating a brand-new allele — a fresh variation that may turn out helpful, harmful, or make no difference.

parts.label: Selection pressure
parts.note: The environment throws a challenge — a predator, cold, or disease — that tests everyone; only the best-suited traits help individuals cope with it.

parts.label: Survivor (best adapted)
parts.note: The best-adapted individuals survive this pressure and reproduce, while poorly-suited ones die out before passing their alleles on.

parts.label: Next generation
parts.note: Survivors pass their helpful alleles to offspring, so the next generation carries more of them — over many generations the whole species shifts.

parts.label: Selective breeding
parts.note: Humans speed this up by choosing individuals with useful traits, like high yield, and breeding them together generation after generation.

parts.label: Fossil evidence
parts.note: Fossils capture how species looked long ago, letting us track gradual changes over time — solid evidence that evolution really happened.

parts.label: Sun (light)
parts.note: It starts with the Sun: its light pours energy into the ecosystem, and how much reaches an area helps decide what can live there.

parts.label: Cactus (adapted)
parts.note: Here a cactus thrives where water is scarce, storing water in its stem and using spines so it wins the fight for survival.

parts.label: Producer
parts.note: The producer, a green plant, traps sunlight to make its own food, feeding itself and everything else that follows in the chain.

parts.label: Herbivore
parts.note: Now a herbivore eats the producer, passing that stored food energy up the chain from plant into animal.

parts.label: Predator
parts.note: Next the predator hunts and eats the herbivore, carrying the energy one more step and controlling how many herbivores there are.

parts.label: Soil & water
parts.note: Underneath, soil and water are the non-living factors supplying minerals and moisture, tying the whole community together into one ecosystem.

parts.label: Carbon dioxide
parts.note: Carbon dioxide floats in the air, the shared pool of carbon that plants pull in and living things breathe back out.

parts.label: Rain cloud
parts.note: Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into this cloud, then falls as rain to water the land below.

parts.label: Plant (photosynthesis)
parts.note: The plant soaks up carbon dioxide and uses sunlight in photosynthesis, locking that carbon into sugars and new growth.

parts.label: Animal
parts.note: Animals eat plants and breathe out carbon dioxide; many different species here mean a stable, healthy ecosystem.

parts.label: Combustion
parts.note: Burning fossil fuels here releases stored carbon dioxide and methane back into the air, warming the planet and harming habitats.

parts.label: Decomposer
parts.note: When plants and animals die, decomposers break them down, freeing nutrients into the soil for new plants to reuse.

parts.label: Element
parts.note: We start pure: every particle here is the same kind of atom, nothing else mixed in. About 100 of these building blocks exist.

parts.label: Compound
parts.note: Now two elements chemically bond together, locking into a brand-new substance whose properties differ completely from the atoms that joined.

parts.label: Mixture
parts.note: Here substances just sit side by side, not bonded, so each keeps its own properties and can be pulled apart physically.

parts.label: Filtration
parts.note: Pour the mixture through paper: the insoluble solid gets trapped as residue while the liquid drains straight through as filtrate.

parts.label: Crystallisation
parts.note: Now gently heat the solution so the solvent evaporates away, leaving the dissolved solid behind as solid crystals forming.

parts.label: Chromatography
parts.note: Solvent creeps up the paper, carrying each substance a different distance, so the mixture spreads into separate coloured spots.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: Right at the centre we pack a tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons; it holds nearly all the atom's mass in a minute space.

parts.label: Proton
parts.note: Inside the nucleus each proton carries a +1 charge and a mass of 1; counting these protons tells us which element the atom is.

parts.label: Neutron
parts.note: Neutrons sit alongside the protons with no charge but a mass of 1, adding weight and helping hold the nucleus together.

parts.label: First Shell
parts.note: Electrons now orbit in shells, filling from the inside out; this first shell fills up first and holds a maximum of 2 electrons.

parts.label: Outer Shell
parts.note: Once the inner shell is full, electrons spill into the next shell out, which can take up to 8, building the arrangement outwards.

parts.label: Electron
parts.note: Each electron carries a -1 charge and almost no mass; in a neutral atom their number matches the protons, so charges cancel out.

parts.label: Increasing atomic number
parts.note: We lay the elements out in order of increasing atomic number, left to right, row by row, so each has one more proton than the last.

parts.label: Group (column)
parts.note: Reading down a column, every element shares the same number of outer electrons, which is why a group behaves in similar ways.

parts.label: Period (row)
parts.note: Moving across a row, we cross a full period, adding one proton and one electron at each step until the shell fills.

parts.label: Metals
parts.note: The left and centre fill with metals, which readily lose electrons, giving them their shine, strength and ability to conduct.

parts.label: Non-metals
parts.note: Over on the right sit the non-metals, which tend to gain or share electrons, behaving quite differently from the metals opposite.

parts.label: Group 1 (alkali metals)
parts.note: Group 1, the alkali metals, throw off their single outer electron to react with water, making hydrogen and an alkali, faster down the group.

parts.label: Group 0 (noble gases)
parts.note: The far-right column is Group 0, the noble gases, whose full outer shells leave nothing to gain or lose, so they stay unreactive.

parts.label: Ionic bond
parts.note: Here a metal hands its outer electrons to a non-metal, making oppositely charged ions that pull together with a strong ionic bond.

parts.label: Covalent bond
parts.note: Between two non-metals, no electrons are given away — instead the atoms share electrons, and this shared pair bonds them together.

parts.label: Shared electron pair
parts.note: This pair of electrons is shared between both atoms, sitting in the middle and pulling the two non-metal nuclei together into one molecule.

parts.label: Positive metal ion
parts.note: In a metal, each atom has lost its outer electrons, leaving a positive metal ion locked in a regular, tightly-packed pattern.

parts.label: Sea of delocalised electrons
parts.note: The lost electrons drift freely around all the ions as a shared sea, gluing the positive ions together and letting metals conduct.

parts.label: Metal loses electron
parts.note: Losing this outer electron leaves the metal atom with a full shell beneath, and a positive charge because it now has more protons than electrons.

parts.label: Giant ionic lattice
parts.note: Millions of oppositely charged ions lock into a giant grid; breaking so many strong bonds needs huge heat, so melting points soar.

parts.label: Simple molecular
parts.note: Only weak forces hold these separate molecules together, so they pull apart easily, giving low melting points and no charge to carry current.

parts.label: Giant covalent
parts.note: Here every atom bonds strongly to its neighbours in one huge network, so enormous heat is needed to break them apart and melt it.

parts.label: Metal structure
parts.note: Positive metal ions sit in a sea of loose electrons that drift freely, carrying charge and heat while layers slide to bend the metal.

parts.label: Alloy (distorted)
parts.note: Mixing in different-sized atoms jams the neat layers so they cannot slide past each other, making the alloy harder than the pure metal.

parts.label: Nanoparticle
parts.note: Shrunk to 1-100 nm, so much surface is exposed for their size that they speed up reactions as catalysts and block UV in sunscreens.

parts.label: Reactivity series
parts.note: We line the metals up from most to least reactive; this ladder predicts every reaction, because a metal higher up displaces one below it from its compound.

parts.label: Very reactive metals
parts.note: At the top sit potassium, sodium, calcium and magnesium; they grab oxygen and other elements eagerly, so they are locked tightly inside compounds in the ground.

parts.label: Unreactive metals
parts.note: Down here copper, silver and gold barely react, so they cling weakly to compounds and are easily pushed out by any metal above them.

parts.label: Carbon's position
parts.note: We slot carbon into the ladder as a dividing line; whether a metal sits above or below it decides how we tear that metal from its ore.

parts.label: Reduction (with carbon)
parts.note: For metals below carbon, like iron, we heat the ore with carbon; carbon steals the oxygen away, reducing the ore back to pure metal.

parts.label: Electrolysis
parts.note: Metals above carbon, like aluminium, hold oxygen too tightly for carbon; instead electricity splits the molten compound apart to release the metal.

parts.label: Power supply (d.c.)
parts.note: The d.c. supply pushes electrons round the circuit, giving one electrode a negative charge and the other a positive charge.

parts.label: Cathode (negative)
parts.note: This electrode is now negative, so it pulls in positive metal ions and hands them electrons, forming the metal here.

parts.label: Anode (positive)
parts.note: This electrode is now positive, so it attracts negative ions and takes electrons from them, forming the non-metal here.

parts.label: Electrolyte
parts.note: Melting or dissolving the compound frees its ions to move, letting charge flow so the compound can be split apart.

parts.label: Positive ion (cation)
parts.note: The positive ion is drawn to the negative cathode, where it gains electrons and turns into a neutral atom.

parts.label: Negative ion (anion)
parts.note: The negative ion is drawn to the positive anode, where it loses electrons and becomes a neutral atom.

parts.label: Energy axis
parts.note: We plot energy going up the side, so we can track how much the reacting particles hold as the reaction runs left to right.

parts.label: Reactants
parts.note: Here sit the starting chemicals, storing their energy before anything reacts; this height is where the whole story begins.

parts.label: Products
parts.note: After reacting, the new substances settle here; where they land compared to the start tells us if energy was released or absorbed.

parts.label: Activation energy
parts.note: Particles must climb this hump first, gaining enough energy on collision to break bonds and get the reaction started.

parts.label: Catalyst path
parts.note: A catalyst carves a lower route over the hump, so more collisions succeed and the reaction speeds up without being used up.

parts.label: Energy change
parts.note: The drop from reactants to products is the energy given out; here products sit lower, so this reaction releases heat overall.

parts.label: Fuel (chemical store)
parts.note: The fuel holds energy in its chemical store. As it burns, that store empties and the energy is released.

parts.label: Boiler (thermal store)
parts.note: The released energy heats water in the boiler — filling its thermal store and boiling it to steam.

parts.label: Turbine
parts.note: The rushing steam pushes the angled blades, so the turbine spins: energy is now in a kinetic store.

parts.label: Generator
parts.note: The spinning turbine turns the generator, which transfers the energy electrically as a current.

parts.label: Pylon (electricity)
parts.note: Pylons carry that current along the wires to homes and factories — the useful output.

parts.label: Wind turbine (renewable)
parts.note: Wind can spin a turbine directly instead of steam — a renewable way to drive the same generator.

parts.label: Bone
parts.note: The bone is stiffened by calcium, giving it the hardness to hold you upright and take your body's weight without bending.

parts.label: Biceps muscle
parts.note: The biceps sits on the front of the upper arm; when it contracts it shortens and pulls the forearm up, bending the elbow.

parts.label: Triceps muscle
parts.note: The triceps lies on the back of the upper arm; it contracts to pull the forearm back down, straightening the elbow again.

parts.label: Tendon
parts.note: A tough tendon anchors the muscle to the bone, so the muscle's pull is passed straight into the bone and moves it.

parts.label: Cartilage
parts.note: Smooth cartilage caps each bone end, cushioning the meeting point and letting the bones slide without grinding against each other.

parts.label: Joint
parts.note: Here two bones meet at a joint; this movable junction is where bending happens as the muscles pull the bones.

parts.label: Ligament
parts.note: Strong ligaments strap the two bones together, holding the joint stable so it bends smoothly without the bones pulling apart.

parts.label: Applied force
parts.note: We draw the push as an arrow: it points the way the force acts, and a longer arrow means a bigger pull in newtons.

parts.label: Extension
parts.note: The force stretches the spring longer; this extra length is the extension, and doubling the force doubles it up to the elastic limit.

parts.label: Weight
parts.note: Gravity pulls the object straight down as weight — a non-contact force acting across a gap, needing nothing to touch it.

parts.label: Pivot
parts.note: The force now turns the object about this fixed pivot; the further out it acts, the bigger the turning moment it makes.

parts.label: Lever arm
parts.note: The long lever arm multiplies the distance from the pivot, so a small push at the end delivers a big turning moment.

parts.label: Resultant force
parts.note: These forces don't cancel, leaving a resultant force that pushes the object into motion in the direction that arrow points.

parts.label: Cell / Battery
parts.note: The cell pushes charge out of one terminal and back into the other; connect both ends to power the loop.

parts.label: Bulb (component)
parts.note: Charge flowing through the bulb makes it light up; this is where the circuit's energy is transferred and used.

parts.label: Resistor
parts.note: The resistor pushes back against the flowing charge; add more resistance and the current drops, so the bulb dims.

parts.label: Voltmeter (across)
parts.note: Wired across the bulb, the voltmeter reads how many volts of energy the charge gives up passing through it.

parts.label: Ammeter (series)
parts.note: Placed in the loop itself, the ammeter counts the charge flowing past each second, reading the current in amps.

parts.label: Conducting wire
parts.note: The metal wire carries the charge round, ferrying energy from the cell to the bulb and back again.

parts.label: Resistance (Ω)
parts.note: Resistance ties it together: current equals potential difference divided by resistance, so voltage and resistance decide the flow.

parts.label: Sunlight
parts.note: Light energy pours down from the Sun. This energy powers the whole reaction, and green chlorophyll traps it inside the leaf.

parts.label: Chloroplast
parts.note: Inside leaf cells sit tiny green chloroplasts. Their chlorophyll captures the sunlight, so this is where photosynthesis actually takes place.

parts.label: Carbon dioxide
parts.note: Carbon dioxide gas drifts in from the air. It is one of two raw ingredients the leaf needs to build sugar.

parts.label: Water
parts.note: Water is pulled up from the roots to the leaf. It joins carbon dioxide as the second reactant fed into the reaction.

parts.label: Oxygen
parts.note: As sugar is built, oxygen is released as waste. It escapes from the leaf into the air for other living things to breathe.

parts.label: Glucose
parts.note: The reaction makes glucose, a sugar. The plant burns it in respiration, builds cell walls, or stores it as starch.

parts.label: Stoma
parts.note: Tiny stomata open on the leaf's underside. Carbon dioxide slips in and oxygen slips out through these gas doorways.

parts.label: pH scale
parts.note: We draw the pH scale as a number line from 0 to 14, measuring how acidic or alkaline any substance is.

parts.label: Neutral (pH 7)
parts.note: Right in the middle sits pH 7, where the substance is neutral, like pure water, neither acid nor alkali.

parts.label: Acid (below 7)
parts.note: Everything below 7 on the left is acidic, so the lower the number, the more strongly acidic the substance becomes.

parts.label: Alkali (above 7)
parts.note: Everything above 7 on the right is alkaline, so the higher the number, the more strongly alkaline it gets.

parts.label: Strong acid (0-2)
parts.note: At the far left, pH 0 to 2, we find strong lab acids; weaker acids like vinegar sit higher at pH 4 to 6.

parts.label: Strong alkali (12-14)
parts.note: At the far right, pH 12 to 14, sit strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide; weak ones like soap sit lower around pH 8 to 10.

parts.label: Universal indicator
parts.note: Adding universal indicator colours the solution: red for strong acids, green at neutral and purple for strong alkalis, revealing its pH.

parts.label: Group 1 (alkali metals)
parts.note: This far-left column holds the alkali metals; reading down the column, each one reacts more violently, so reactivity climbs as you go.

parts.label: Metals
parts.note: Most of the table fills with metals: strong, shiny, bendy conductors of heat and electricity, so the vast bulk of elements sit on this side.

parts.label: Metal / non-metal divide
parts.note: This zig-zag line splits the table: metals on the left give basic oxides, while non-metals on the right form mostly acidic oxides.

parts.label: Non-metals
parts.note: Squeezed into the top-right corner sit the roughly 18 non-metals: brittle, dull insulators that behave the opposite way to metals.

parts.label: Group 0 (noble gases)
parts.note: The final column holds the noble gases; their outer shells are already full, so they barely react and drift about as loners.

parts.label: Period (row)
parts.note: Reading across a row is a period; the properties shift steadily from reactive metal on the left to unreactive gas on the right.

parts.label: Group 7 (halogens)
parts.note: This column holds the halogens; unlike Group 1, going down makes them less reactive, so the top one grabs electrons most fiercely.

parts.label: Distance axis
parts.note: This upward axis tracks distance travelled. As we climb it, the object has moved further from its starting point.

parts.label: Time axis
parts.note: Time runs along the bottom, ticking forward second by second. Reading left to right, we watch the journey unfold.

parts.label: Moving (slope)
parts.note: The line climbs as time passes, so distance grows each second. That sloping rise tells us the object is on the move.

parts.label: Stationary (flat)
parts.note: Here the line goes flat: time passes but distance stops growing, so the object has halted and is standing still.

parts.label: Faster (steeper)
parts.note: Now the line rockets up steeply, covering lots of distance per second. A steeper slope always means a faster object.

parts.label: Ovary
parts.note: Here, once a month, the ovary ripens and releases a single ovum, ready to begin its journey and possibly be fertilised.

parts.label: Oviduct
parts.note: The ovum travels down the oviduct, and it is here that a sperm's nucleus fuses with it to form a zygote.

parts.label: Sperm
parts.note: Sperm swim up using their tails, powered by mitochondria, then use enzymes to break into the ovum's outer layer.

parts.label: Placenta
parts.note: At the placenta, oxygen and nutrients diffuse from mother to fetus while waste passes back the other way to be removed.

parts.label: Umbilical cord
parts.note: The umbilical cord is the lifeline carrying blood between fetus and placenta, ferrying supplies in and waste out.

parts.label: Fetus
parts.note: The growing fetus develops here, cushioned by amniotic fluid that absorbs knocks and keeps it safe until birth.

parts.label: North pole
parts.note: One end of the magnet is the north pole, where the magnetism is concentrated and pulling power is at its strongest.

parts.label: South pole
parts.note: The opposite end is the south pole; every magnet always has both, and a north will attract this south.

parts.label: Field line
parts.note: Invisible field lines loop out from north and curve back into south, crowding tightest at the poles where the field is strongest.

parts.label: Iron object
parts.note: A steel object contains iron, so the field grabs it and pulls it towards the magnet across the gap.

parts.label: Compass
parts.note: The compass needle is a tiny magnet that swings until it lines up with Earth's iron-nickel field, pointing north.

parts.label: Solenoid (coil)
parts.note: Coiling wire into a solenoid and switching on a current builds an electromagnet you can strengthen with more turns or turn off.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: The nucleus is the control centre — it holds the genetic material and directs everything the cell does.

parts.label: Cell membrane
parts.note: A thin cell membrane wraps the whole cell, controlling what is allowed in and out.

parts.label: Cytoplasm
parts.note: Inside, jelly-like cytoplasm fills the cell; this is where most of its chemical reactions happen.

parts.label: Mitochondria
parts.note: Dotted through the cytoplasm are the mitochondria, where respiration releases energy from food.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: Start at the centre: the tiny, dense nucleus holds the protons and neutrons, and nearly all the atom's mass.

parts.label: Electron
parts.note: Around it sit the much lighter electrons, moving in the space surrounding the nucleus.

parts.label: Electron shell
parts.note: The electrons are arranged in shells — fixed energy levels at set distances from the nucleus.

parts.label: Bulb
parts.note: Add a bulb; when current flows through it, it lights up, transferring energy to the surroundings.

parts.label: Cell (battery)
parts.note: Start with the cell — it pushes the current around the circuit, supplying the energy.

parts.label: Switch
parts.note: A switch controls the loop — closed, it lets current flow; open, it breaks the circuit and the bulb goes out.

parts.label: Cell wall
parts.note: A plant cell has a stiff cell wall outside the membrane, giving it a fixed shape and support.

parts.label: Nucleus
parts.note: Like an animal cell, it has a nucleus controlling the cell and holding its genetic material.

parts.label: Permanent vacuole
parts.note: A large permanent vacuole in the middle is full of sap, pushing outwards to keep the cell firm.

parts.label: Chloroplast
parts.note: Green chloroplasts trap light energy so the plant can make its own food by photosynthesis.

parts.label: Eyepiece lens
parts.note: This is the eyepiece — the lens you look down. It magnifies the image a little before it reaches your eye.

parts.label: Objective lens
parts.note: Just above the slide sits the objective lens. You swap between objectives to choose how magnified the image is.

parts.label: Stage
parts.note: The slide clips onto the flat stage, holding your specimen still in the path of the light.

parts.label: Mirror
parts.note: A mirror at the bottom reflects light up through the specimen, so it looks bright when you look down.

parts.label: Solid
parts.note: In a solid the particles are packed in a fixed, regular pattern, touching and only able to vibrate on the spot.

parts.label: Liquid
parts.note: Warm it to a liquid and the particles stay touching, but can now slide past each other in a random jumble.

parts.label: Gas
parts.note: Heat it more and the particles break free — in a gas they are far apart and move quickly in every direction.

parts.label: Biceps
parts.note: The biceps runs along the front of the upper arm; when it contracts it shortens and pulls the forearm up.

parts.label: Triceps
parts.note: The triceps lies on the back; it contracts to straighten the arm, pulling the opposite way to the biceps.

parts.label: Tendon
parts.note: Tough tendons anchor each muscle to the bone, so when the muscle pulls, the bone moves with it.

parts.label: Trachea
parts.note: Air enters down the trachea, the windpipe leading from your throat into the chest.

parts.label: Bronchus
parts.note: The trachea splits into two bronchi, one carrying air into each lung.

parts.label: Alveoli
parts.note: The bronchi branch into millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, where gases pass into and out of the blood.

parts.label: Diaphragm
parts.note: Below the lungs sits the diaphragm, a sheet of muscle that flattens to pull air in and relaxes to push it out.

parts.label: Oesophagus
parts.note: Food is swallowed and squeezed down the oesophagus, the muscular tube leading to the stomach.

parts.label: Liver
parts.note: The liver makes bile, which breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones so they are easier to digest.

parts.label: Stomach
parts.note: In the stomach, acid and muscular churning break the food down into a soupy mixture.

parts.label: Small intestine
parts.note: In the small intestine the digested food is absorbed into the blood through its thin, folded wall.

parts.label: Crest
parts.note: The crest is the highest point of the wave — the top of each hump.

parts.label: Trough
parts.note: The trough is the lowest point — the dip between two crests.

parts.label: Wavelength
parts.note: The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next: one complete wave.

parts.label: Amplitude
parts.note: The amplitude is the height from the middle rest line up to a crest; a bigger amplitude carries more energy.

parts.label: Normal
parts.note: Draw the normal — an imaginary line at 90° to the mirror where the ray hits. Every angle is measured from it.

parts.label: Incident ray
parts.note: The incident ray is the light travelling in towards the mirror.

parts.label: Reflected ray
parts.note: The reflected ray leaves on the other side of the normal at the same angle: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

parts.label: Mirror
parts.note: Light meets the shiny surface of the mirror, which bounces it back instead of letting it pass through.

parts.label: Weight
parts.note: Weight pulls the object straight down — the force of gravity acting on its mass.

parts.label: Reaction force
parts.note: The surface pushes straight back up with an equal reaction force, which stops the object sinking through it.

parts.label: Push (applied force)
parts.note: An applied push or pull acts in the direction you are trying to move the object.

parts.label: Friction
parts.note: Friction acts along the surface in the opposite direction to the motion, trying to slow the object down.

parts.label: Producer (grass)
parts.note: Every food chain starts with a producer like grass, which makes its own food using light energy.

parts.label: Prey (rabbit)
parts.note: The arrow points to the rabbit, the prey that eats the producer and takes in its energy.

parts.label: Predator (fox)
parts.note: At the end, the predator (a fox) eats the prey — energy passes along the chain with every arrow.

parts.label: Skull
parts.note: The skull is the hard bony case that surrounds and protects the brain.

parts.label: Ribcage
parts.note: The ribcage forms a protective basket around the heart and lungs.

parts.label: Spine
parts.note: The spine is a column of small bones that holds you upright and shields the spinal cord.

parts.label: Femur (thigh bone)
parts.note: The femur, or thigh bone, is the body's longest, strongest bone and carries your weight when you stand.
